prompt.es: Escucha el programa y elige qué consejo final da la experta.

choices.text: Use the most formal phrase available, since politeness covers any length of pause.
Acknowledge that the question is hard, then reason aloud so the pause has content.
Rely on the informal phrase, since listeners forgive casual wording more than silence.
Fill every pause with short fillers, because silence always sounds like anxiety.

feedback.es: La experta recomienda combinar dos recursos: decir que la pregunta es difícil y pensar en voz alta, porque el oyente perdona una pausa antes que una respuesta vacía.

origin.audio: On the show, a speaking coach described three ways to buy time and ranked them by register. Hang on, she said, works among friends but sounds curt in a formal meeting. That's a tricky question is neutral, and useful because it flatters the questioner while you think. Allow me a moment to consider that is the most formal, yet it carries a risk: if the pause that follows is too long, politeness turns into anxiety. Her advice was to combine two of them, naming the difficulty and then thinking out loud, because listeners forgive a pause far more easily than they forgive an empty reply.

prompt.es: ¿Qué da a entender la coordinadora sobre el candidato?

choices.text: That the speed of his reply counted in his favour, since it showed confidence.
That the question was unfair, since nobody could have answered it well.
That the speed of his reply counted against him, since it hid how he reasons.
That the panel would have preferred a long silence to any spoken answer.

feedback.es: La coordinadora lamenta que, al responder al instante, no dejó ver cómo razona; su rapidez jugó en su contra, y no se cuestiona la pregunta ni se pide un silencio largo.

origin.text: Thanks for sitting in on the last interview. The candidate answered the surprise question at once, before the chair had finished speaking, and the answer was careless. Two seconds of silence would have told us how he reasons, which is exactly what we were hoping to assess. Instead, three panel members wrote the same comment in their notes: no sign of judgement.

es: Identificar el punto, la razón, el ejemplo y el cierre en respuestas improvisadas, reconocer tangentes y decidir cuál de varias respuestas está mejor ordenada y por qué.

teaching.en: A well-built answer opens with the point, stated in one sentence: my point is that cities need more bike lanes.
teaching.es: Una respuesta bien construida empieza por el punto, dicho en una frase: mi punto es que las ciudades necesitan más ciclovías.
teaching.explanationEs: El punto es tu postura, dicha en una sola frase y al principio.

teaching.audioText: A well-built answer opens with the point, stated in one sentence: my point is that cities need more bike lanes.

teaching.en: The main reason should follow at once, because an opinion with no reason gives the listener nothing to weigh.

with no reason gives the listener nothing to weigh.

teaching.en: Then add an example, such as accidents falling in my neighbourhood after the new lane opened, to drive the point home.
teaching.es: Después añade un ejemplo, como que los accidentes bajaron en mi barrio cuando se abrió la nueva ciclovía, para dejar clara la idea.
teaching.explanationEs: El ejemplo apoya la razón con un caso concreto; drive the point home = dejarlo claro.
segments: Then add an example, such as accidents falling in my neighbourhood

teaching.en: Close with a conclusion that repeats your point in fresh words rather than introducing a brand-new idea.

teaching.explanationEs: El cierre devuelve al oyente a tu punto, no abre otro tema.
segments: Close with a conclusion that repeats your point in

origin.text: My point is that buses should be free. The main reason is that they reduce traffic. For instance, my town tried it for a month, and the roads were much quieter. In conclusion, free buses benefit everyone.

origin.audio: The teacher asked three students whether school should start later. The first student said that he liked sleeping, that his brother never woke up on time and that mornings were, well, a bit grey, and then he trailed off. The second said that her point was yes; the main reason was that teenagers need more sleep; for example, her cousin's grades had improved after his school changed its hours; and in conclusion, later starts help everyone. The third said that her point was yes, that the main reason was that teenagers need sleep, and that, in conclusion, schools should start later.

prompt.es: Responde a la pregunta sorpresa en un minuto, con las cuatro partes.

answer.text: That's a tricky one, so let me think for a second. My stance is that a generalist has more options than a specialist. The main reason is that jobs change faster than any single specialist can follow. A generalist can move between fields, learn new tools and adapt when a company changes direction. For example, my cousin trained as a nurse, then worked in a hospital office, and now manages a small clinic. If she had stayed only a specialist, she would not have had those chances. Of course, specialists are important, and I would not want a generalist to be my doctor. Sorry, I'm rambling a little; let me get back to my point. In the end, it boils down to this: you want a specialist when lives are at stake and a generalist when the ground keeps moving. So, in short, I would rather be a generalist with one strong skill, because that mix gives me both skill and choices.
accepted: That's a tricky one, so let me think for a second. My stance is that a generalist has more options than a specialist. The main reason is that jobs change faster than any single specialist can follow. A generalist can move between fields, learn new tools and adapt when a company changes direction. For example, my cousin trained as a nurse, then worked in a hospital office, and now manages a small clinic. If she had stayed only a specialist, she would not have had those chances. Of course, specialists are important, and I would not want a generalist to be my doctor. Sorry, I'm rambling a little; let me get back to my point. In the end, it boils down to this: you want a specialist when lives are at stake and a generalist when the ground keeps moving. So, in short, I would rather be a generalist with one strong skill, because that mix gives me both skill and choices.

Let me think for a moment. I would say that specialists are better, so my stance is clear. The first reason is that experts solve hard problems faster. A specialist has spent years on one subject, and companies pay more for that skill. For example, my uncle is an engineer who only repairs bridges, and he is always busy because nobody else can do his job. Some people say that a generalist is more flexible, and that is true. However, I think being flexible without real skill is risky, because a generalist may never learn anything well. That is why I prefer to commit to one field and to learn it thoroughly. To sum up, I believe that a specialist has the advantage, and I would advise young people to choose one area and to become really good at it.

origin.audio: After the timer stopped, the coach played back a student's answer. The student had begun well: a short pause, then a clear stance on whether the school day should start later. The reason was convincing, and the example, about her brother falling asleep in his first lesson, was vivid. But with ten seconds left she remembered a second example and began telling it, and the minute ended before she could close. The coach did not question the content. She pointed at the clock and said that an answer without a closing sentence is like a story without its last line.

answer.text: Thanks, that's a tricky first question, so let me think. My stance is that students should wear a uniform. The main reason is that it saves time and money. For example, I spend ten minutes every morning deciding what to wear at weekends, but only two on school days. Sorry, I meant five on school days. In short, a uniform is a useful habit. Second question. Hang on, let me gather my thoughts. I would say that studying in a group is better than studying alone, because ideas travel faster. For example, last month my group solved a hard problem in an hour that I had failed to solve alone in an evening. Let me rephrase that: a group gives you a second mind. Third question, what would I change in my school? Off the top of my head, I would open the library on Saturdays. The reason is that many students have no quiet place at home. To recap, uniforms save time, groups save effort and an open library saves weekends. My point is that small changes matter.

origin.audio: In the final of the radio quiz, the host threw a surprise round at the three contestants. The first, rattled by the opening question, hesitated for so long that her time ran out. The second kept his composure, bought a few seconds with a joke and gave a structured answer, but he mixed up two dates and had to repair them twice. The third gave a slower, plainer answer; when she stumbled, she rephrased instead of stopping, and closed with a one-sentence recap. The audience cheered her the loudest, and the host admitted that she had won the round before the scores were read out.

origin.text: Note to the presenter: in tonight's rapid-fire round, please do not rush the contestants. Several of them began well but lost their way when the next question came too quickly.
